# Chapter 17 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) R1 and R3 touch customer data: Any residual at high is above the line -
must be treated, and acceptance of their (low) residuals belongs to management
or the board, not a team lead. R2 is availability: One hour per quarter is the
drawn line, so a residual meaning rare, short outages could be accepted - by
management, since it touches the stated appetite; a marketing-site defacement
risk at medium is the operations lead's to sign. (2) Missing: The residual
level, the explicit decision wording, the accepter's name and role (with
authority matching R2's size), the date, and the review trigger. Repaired: R2
residual - DDoS outage after basic filtering; level: Medium (possible $\times$
major); decision: Accept; accepted by: Managing director, 20 Oct 2026; review
trigger: Any outage over 30 minutes, or 12 months. (3) Protection is *reduce*
(lowers likelihood and duration); insurance is *transfer* (moves the financial
loss, not the outage or the customers' experience); doing nothing is acceptance
- above the appetite, so not available. Recommend reduce: The appetite is
stated in downtime, and only protection buys downtime; the residual is a
determined attack exceeding the scrubbing capacity - rarer, shorter, and now
insurable as a second layer if wanted. (4) Summary: Database-breach risk is high
(possible $\times$ disastrous); encryption at rest cuts the impact of R3
decisively - approve EUR 7k. Decision needed: Approve EUR 7k for database
encryption; owner IT lead; live in four weeks; residual to be re-evaluated and
formally accepted on completion. (5) KPI: Share of customer-data stores
encrypted with current keys - a fall triggers an implementation review. KRI 1
(review trigger): Privileged accounts with direct database access - crossing
the agreed ceiling reopens the acceptance. KRI 2: Unpatched criticals on
database-adjacent systems - a rise means the exposure is growing ahead of
incidents, so patching is pulled forward.
